title: Computational setup
text:
In this course, you will learn how to analyse sequencing data (both RNA-seq and genome sequencing). These kinds of datasets require specialized software to be processed, which are typically run on Linux servers. Therefore, we will make use of a command-line interface (CLI) on the Crunchomics compute cluster of the University of Amsterdam. Command-line interfaces are an alternative to graphical user interface, with which you are probably more familiar. The contents of this course are tailored to students who may have never used a command-line interface before. You need to take a few simple steps to connect to Crunchomics.

One software that is running on the Crunchomics server is RStudio, which you should be familiar with. To connect to the RStudio server, open an internet browser window (e.g. Google Chrome) and go to https://omics-app01.science.uva.nl/
After signing on with your usual UvA password, you should see the familiar RStudio environment in your browser:


In the bottom-left panel, you see three tabs: Console, Terminal and Background Jobs. Click on Terminal to bring it to the foreground.


In this terminal, type the following command. Replace YOURSTUDENTNUMBER with….. your student number 😃.

ssh YOURSTUDENTNUMBER@omics-h0.science.uva.nl
Now you are connected to the Crunchomics “headnode”, where you can run all sorts of software. You will need to do these steps every time you sign into the headnode to run programs.

Again in the terminal, type the following two commands to properly initialize your account (you only need to run these commands once):

/zfs/omics/software/script/omics_install_script
and
/zfs/omics/software/script/omics_mv_rstudio_cache
That’s it! You are now ready to start working on Crunchomics. Let’s take a moment to recap what we did:

We used the red route on the left-hand side on this schematic to connect to the Crunchomics application server (via the blue “AAS” arrow). To reach the headnode (h0) we used a ssh (the dark green arrow) command on the terminal. You can also directly connect to the headnode by using an ssh connection from a command line on your local computer (terminal app for Mac users, MobaXterm or other options for Windows users). You can also see that both the application server and the headnode have access to the Crunchomics storage server. Finally, there are 5 ‘compute nodes’ on Crunchomics; this is where large computations can be sent to via a job submission system (we will not use this system in this course, unfortunately!).
In the next episode we will learn the basics of navigating the filesystem on your Crunchomics account. We will do this on the command line only!

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
During the setup, you already ran some first commands. In this episode, we will learn a handful of very useful basic unix commands to navigate your filesystem, to move around files, and to inspect the content of files. If you’re logged in to the head node, you should see something like this:
It shows your user name (mpaauw), the name of the node we are connected to (omics-h0), and after the $ sign, a blinking cursor. That’s where we will start typing commands to interact with the filesystem.

title: Introduction to the command line
section: pwd: find out where we are
text:
pwd: find out where we are
Let’s orient ourselves by typing our first command, pwd, into the terminal, and pressing enter.
pwd
pwd prints the location of the current working directory and tells you where exactly you are in the file system. In my case, this prints /home/mpaauw as output.

title: Introduction to the command line
section: ls: list the contents of a directory
text:
ls: list the contents of a directory
Now that we know where we are, let’s find out what files and folders exist in our home directory. For this, you can use the ls command, which lists the contents of the directory you are currently in:
ls
If you set-up you Crunchomics account correctly, you should see a folder called personal. That’s where you can store up to 500GB of data on Crunchomics. Try adding the following modifier, or flag, to the ls command to change the output format:

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
cd: moving between directories
To be able to use the personal directory, we have to move in there. The command cd exists to do just that. Essentially, it’s equivalent to clicking on a directory in the file navigation system on your own computer.
cd personal/
Let’s verify that we actually ended up in this personal folder:
pwd
Should now print /home/mpaauw/personal.
You can move back ‘up’ in the hierarchy of directories by running:
cd ..

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
mkdir: make new folders
We can also make new folders. Let’s navigate into personal again, and create a folder that will contain all the code and data for the Molecular Data Analysis module. We’ll abbreviate it to MDA.
cd personal/

mkdir MDA






Exercise






Verify that the MDA directory was created.
Navigate into it.
Verify that you are now working in the MDA directory.
Inspect the contents of the MDA directory.
Within MDA, create another directory, called intro-to-cli, and navigate into it.



Click me to see the answer
# 1. Yes, I see the MDA folder now!
ls

# 2. Let's navigate into it
cd MDA/

# 3. This should print confirmation that you are now in MDA
pwd

# 4. This folder should be empty
ls

# 5. 
mkdir intro-to-cli
cd intro-to-cli/

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
wget: download data
Next, let’s download some sequencing data. We will use the wget command to download some sequencing data from a repository, into the currect working directory.
wget https://github.com/mishapaauw/molecular-data-analysis/blob/main/part0-setup/data/sample1.fastq.gz
As always, verify that your file arrived by running ls.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
cp: copying data
When doing bioinformatics projects, a clear folder structure is essential to keep yourself organized. We will copy the data to a new folder that we call data.
mkdir data

cp sample1.fastq.gz data/

# Verify that it worked
ls -l
ls -l data
You should see that we now have two copies of the .fastq data. One file is in the working directory, and the other one is in the data folder. Notice that we added a flag, or option, to the ls command: -l. This specifies that the output is now presented in a list format.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
rm: remove files and folders
We only need one copy of the data: let’s remove the sequencing data that is now stored in our working directory with a new command rm.
rm sample1.fastq.gz

# check if it worked
ls -l 






Important



Unix does not have an undelete command, a trash can, or a bin
This means that if you delete something with rm, it’s gone. Therefore, use rm with care and check what you write twice before pressing enter!

title: Introduction to the command line
section: history: keeping track of what you did
text:
history: keeping track of what you did
The history command is quite useful: it keeps a list of all the commands that you used today. You can view this as a simple automated labjournal, although it does not contain any output, or information whether a command worked at all.






Exercise






Remove the sequencing data from the data folder as well.
Use history to find back the command to download the data.
Redownload the data, and this time, move (mv) the data to the data folder.
Use ls commands to inspect what happened by using mv rather than cp.



Click me to see the answer
# 1. Oh no, I removed my raw data!
rm data/sample1.fastq.gz

# 2. Ah, I remember, it was the wget command.
history

# 3. Let's download again, and this time move it instead of copy
wget https://github.com/mishapaauw/molecular-data-analysis/raw/refs/heads/main/part0-setup/data/sample1.fastq.gz
mv sample1.fastq.gz data/

# 4. Now we only have one copy of the data, in the data folder.
ls -l
ls -l data/





Instead of retyping commands, you can also press the arrow ‘up’ key to cycle through commands you already ran before.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
gunzip: uncompress files
You may have noticed that the file with sequencing data has.gz as file extension. This means that the file is compressed, or zipped. This saves storage space. While many bioinformatics tools can deal with compressed files, we will uncompress it to be able to inspect the file.
gunzip data/sample1.fastq.gz

ls data/
This should now show that you have a single file in the data/ folder: sample1.fastq.

title: Introduction to the command line
section: head, tail, and cat: inspecting the contents of a file
text:
head, tail, and cat: inspecting the contents of a file
Many bioinformatics files, including .fastq files, are essentially just text files. We will learn a few more command to inspect files on the terminal. After all, we can’t just open them in Notepad.

head: view the first 10 rows of a file
head data/sample1.fastq


tail: view the first 10 rows of a file
tail data/sample1.fastq


cat: view the full file
Warning! Your terminal will just print everything if you ask it to. If your file is huge, this may take a while. If you’re stuck in such a situation, you can always hits control + C to break out of it.
cat data/sample1.fastq

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
grep: searching things
Each read is represented by four rows in a .fastq file. First, there’s the read header (or name, if you want). Then, there’s the actual sequence. Finally, there’s a spacer row and a row with quality encoding (more on that in a later episode!). Let’s say we are only interested in the read name and their sequence at this point. We can use grep to search for patterns (much like you’d use control + F in a Word file on your computer!).
As you may have seen, each read name starts with @ERR. We can use that to search:
grep @ERR data/sample1.fastq
And voila, we get just the read headers printed to our terminal.
We can also ask grep to report the first line after a search hit by adding the -A 1 option (likewise, we could ask for a line before a search hit: -B 1).
grep @ERR data/sample1.fastq -A 1

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
wc: counting things
We might be interested in the number of reads in our .fastq file. We know now that each read takes four rows; if we could find out the number of rows we could calculate the number of reads! The wc (word count) command does just that, if we specify that we are interested in lines (-l).
wc -l data/sample1.fastq 
Okay, there are 200,000 rows. So there must be 50,000 reads in this dataset!

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
| and >: creating litle pipelines
It would be nice to find out the number of reads in a dataset without having to do a manual calculation. We have the tools to do so: we could grep for @ERR, giving us a list of just the read headers, and then count the number of lines using wc -l. We just need to learn how to string them together. In command-line interfaces, this is called ‘piping’ and is done with the | symbol. Let’s try.
grep '@ERR' data/sample1.fastq | wc -l
50,000! This command directly prints the answer to your terminal. What happens is that the list of read headers is redirected into the wc -l command, instead of being printed to the terminal.
We can add one more step to this pipeline and save this number to a file to keep for later reference:
grep '@ERR' data/sample1.fastq | wc -l > number_of_reads.txt

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
seqkit: sequence file manipulation
We can do a lot with a small set of basic terminal commands, but luckily, people have developed tools to make working with sequencing files easier. One of such tools is seqkit, which has numerous ‘sub-commands’.
seqkit stats data/sample1.fastq 
This confirms that we have 50,000 sequences, and additionaly, we learn that the reads are 101 basepairs long.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
Exercises






Exercise





Sometimes, sequencing reads can still contain the adapter sequences that are ligated to the DNA molecules before sequencing. A fragment of the Illumina TruSeq adapter that you might find is AGATCGGAAGAGC. Since these fragments do not contain biological information, reads with adapter fragments are considered ‘contaminated’ and should be cleaned or removed.

Search for the adapter sequence using grep. How many times do find the adapter sequence in this dataset? And where do you find the adapters in the reads?



Click me to see the answer
grep AGATCGGAAGAGC data/sample1.fastq # the adapters are located at the start or the end of the reads, never somewhere in the middle.
grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC data/sample1.fastq # 51 hits!



Add the read headers for the contaminated reads, by modifying your grep command.



Click me to see the answer
grep AGATCGGAAGAGC data/sample1.fastq -B 1



Now, pipe | these results into a new command to just get the headers and get rid of the sequences.



Click me to see the answer
grep AGATCGGAAGAGC data/sample1.fastq -B 1 | grep ERR



Clean up the read headers. For now we are just interested in the read ID; that’s any information that starts with the @ sign until the first space. Hint: you will need the cut command, which we have not yet learned. Use man cut to read the official documentation, or search online.



Click me to see the answer
grep AGATCGGAAGAGC data/sample1.fastq -B 1 | grep ERR | cut -f 1 -d ' '



Finally, save the output of this pipeline into a file called contaminated_reads.txt.



Click me to see the answer
grep AGATCGGAAGAGC data/sample1.fastq -B 1 | grep ERR | cut -f 1 -d ' ' > contaminated_reads.txt











Exercise





seqkit can be used to filter reads by average quality scores. Run the following command: seqkit seq --min-qual 25 data/sample1.fastq.

You will see that the high-quality reads are printed to your terminal. That’s not very useful, store the results into a new file called sample1-HQ-reads.fastq



Click me to see the answer
seqkit seq --min-qual 25 data/sample1.fastq > data/sample1-HQ.fastq



Count the number of reads that passed the quality filtering step.



Click me to see the answer
seqkit stats data/sample1-HQ.fastq # 38,416 reads survived



Try running the following code seqkit stats data/sample1*.fastq. Discuss with your neighbour what the * character is doing in this command.



Click me to see the answer
seqkit stats data/sample1*.fastq
processed files:  2 / 2 [======================================] ETA: 0s. done
file                   format  type  num_seqs    sum_len  min_len  avg_len  max_len
data/sample1.fastq     FASTQ   DNA     50,000  5,050,000      101      101      101
data/sample1-HQ.fastq  FASTQ   DNA     38,416  3,880,016      101      101      101
# It looks like the wildcard helped seqkit to find both fastq files!

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
Wrap-up
That’s it for today. You just learned a handful of commands to work in a command-line environment. Although the commands are simple, combining them into small pipelines they can become very powerful tools to manipulate and analyze text files. In the following tutorials, we will start learning more specialized bioinformatics commands.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
Credits
Materials for this episode were strongly inspired by, and partly copied from, Nina Dombrowski’s ‘Introduction to the cli’ tutorial.

title: Episode 1: Reproducible science using Github
text:
You may have heard of the FAIR principle for research data: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable. These principles focus on how you manage your data, scripts, and results. Adhering to these principles makes tracking and sharing your work easier. You can imagine that a script sitting somewhere on your computer fails FAIR on nearly all aspects: nobody else can find it, access it, or reuse it: and a year from now, neither can you. git and Github address this directly. Putting the data and scripts of your analysis under ‘version control’ gives you a timestamped history of every change that you made. Pushing that history to Github makes it accessible for others.
Today we will setup a Github repository and push an analysis to it, from the cluster.

title: Episode 1: Reproducible science using Github
text:
Setting up a repository

Make a GitHub account Go to github.com → Sign up → follow the prompts
Make a repository on GitHub

Click the + (top right) → New repository
Name it (e.g. `data_visualization_episode)
Leave it Public, tick Add a README
Create repository


Github is very serious about safety. This is good, but it forces us to use a bit more complicate authentication methods than just a password.

Generate a Personal Access Token (your “password” when committing changes).

Log in → click your profile picture (top right) → Settings
Left sidebar, scroll down → Developer settings
Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic)
Generate new token (classic)
Name: bioinformatics · Expiration: 14 days · Check the box: repo
Generate token → copy it now (you won’t see it again) → paste it somewhere safe (e.g. a text file) for later

title: Episode 1: Reproducible science using Github
section: Cloning the repository to the cluster

title: Episode 1: Reproducible science using Github
section: Adding a new file and committing it.
text:
Adding a new file and committing it.
Let’s make a data directory, and add a data file to it:
mkdir data
wget -O data/penguins.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv
First we verify that we actually have the dataset:
ls data/
It’s really there! Now, we can run git status to verify that git is actually also aware that the file now exists in our repository. But, git is not yet keeping track of this file.
1git status
2git add .
3git status
4git commit -m "added pinguins dataset"
5git push

1

git sees that the file is there, but it’s not being tracked.

2

Let’s add all files to the git tracking!

3

Yes, now git has ‘staged’ the data file.

4

Now we ‘commit’ the file

5

The final step is pushing the changes to github.

title: Molecular Data Analysis & Bioinformatics
text: This module is designed to equip you with essential computational skills for modern biological research, from data visualization to advanced genomics analyses. Throughout this module, you’ll work with real-world datasets and well-known bioinformatics tools, to build a strong foundation in reproducible computational biology.

title: Molecular Data Analysis & Bioinformatics
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Create publication-quality data visualizations using R packages
Perform RNA-seq analysis, from mapping raw reads to differential expression analysis
Integrate RNA-seq results into a research project with a biological question
Perform a genome assembly, and assess the quality of the resulting assembly
Document and communicate your analyses effectively

title: Molecular Data Analysis & Bioinformatics
text:
Module structure
This module is organized into three parts, and there’s a setup section (‘part 0’):

Part 0: Setup: Before diving into the analyses, you’ll configure your computational environment with all necessary software, packages, and dependencies.
Part 1: Data visualization in R: Starting with the basics: data visualization using ggplot2 in R. In addition, we will work on making our science reproducible using Github.
Part 2: RNA-seq analysis: Explore transcriptomics through an RNA-seq workflow.
Part 3: Genome assembly: Explore the challenges of reconstructing genomes from sequencing reads.

Indeed, the are 344 observations. We have some categorical data encoded as factors (species, island, sex) and some measurements of the bodies of the penguins (bill_len, flipper_len).
To make a bar plot, we first need to calculate the mean and standard error. In this case, we will group by species, and calculate the mean body_mass:
R

penguins_summary <- penguins %>% 
  group_by(species) %>% 
  summarize(mean = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
            se = sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()))

title: Episode 2: Data visualisation
section: From bar plot to sina plot
text:
From bar plot to sina plot
Let’s visualise the mean body mass using a ‘traditional’ barplot with error bars.



R

penguins_summary %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = mean)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2)









It does show what we just discovered, but it hides a lot. The standard error bars give some sort of idea of the spread of the data, but what does the spread really look like? A boxplot helps to solve this proble, at least partially:



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_boxplot()









Instead of the mean, boxplots highlight the median value (thick line), the 25% and 75% percentile value (the box), and 15 * IQR (the lines) (where IQR is the inter-quartile range, or distance between the first and third quartiles). It’s better, but it still hides the actual data. Let’s add each individual datapoint. To do this, we use geom_jitter() to add a little bit of noise in the x-axis direction:



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5)









This is nice, but we can let the shape that we’re plotting follow the distribution of the underlying datapoints rather than just plot boxes. The boxplots then become violin plots:



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5)









This is an improvement, but the points don’t follow their distribution very well. We can change that by moving from geom_jitter to geom_quasirandom, from the ggbeeswarm package. The combination of violin plot with individual datapoints that follow their distribution is called a sina plot.



R

library(ggbeeswarm)

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_quasirandom(alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2)









This is starting to become an honest, information dense plot. However, the default choice of y-axis range exaggerates the difference in body mass between Gentoo penguins and the other species.



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_quasirandom(alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA))









Let’s now work a bit on the visuals. To achieve a higher data-to-ink ratio, we remove the grey background and most grid lines:



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_quasirandom(alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
   labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",  
    axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.4),  
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
  )

title: Episode 2: Data visualisation
text:
Simpson’s Paradox
Simpson’s paradox is a phenomenon in data visualisation where a trend appears in aggregated groups of data, but disappears or even reverses when grouping information is taken into account. palmerpenguins contains a beatiful example of Simpson’s paradox:



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = FALSE) +
  theme_classic()









Okay, so, the bill depth is negatively correlated to the bill length! Let’s color the points by species, just to make sure this is correct.



R

penguins %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_classic()









Woah!

title: Episode 2: Data visualisation
text:
Assignment






Assignment



You have learned what makes a good visualization. Now do the opposite: make the worst possible figure from the palmerpenguins dataset. Aim to commit as many of these ‘data visualisation sins’ as you can:

Hide the truth:

Use a barplot with no indication of spread or sample size
Pool across species or sex to hide real patterns
Truncate the y-axis to exaggerate tiny differences

Use unclear visuals:

Use clashing, non-colorblind-friendly colors
Leave axis labels as raw column names, give the plot a misleading title
Map the same variable to color, shape, and size simultaneously

Produce this plot in 1 code chunk, save it as a .png file.
knit your .Rmd file, push all changes to Github.
Add you plot into the shared Google Presentations sheet, and add three bullet points describing why your plot is the most ugly and misleading plot ever made.
